segments.heading: Today's brief
segments.speak: Good morning. This is your startup brief for Thursday, 3 September 2026. Today we have 8 companies: Abridge, Mirendil, SUN, Sazabi, Superset, Ezra, Kira, and Librar Labs. Each one takes about a minute. I will tell you what they do, what traction they have, why it matters, and one thing you could steal from them for your own idea. Let's go.

segments.heading: Abridge
segments.subhead: Andreessen Horowitz · a16z-led Series E · Healthcare AI
segments.speak: Number 1 of 8. Abridge. Listens to the doctor's appointment and writes the medical note. Andreessen Horowitz, Andreessen Horowitz-led Series E. Abridge is ambient AI for clinicians. It sits in the room, listens to the conversation between doctor and patient, and produces the clinical documentation, so the doctor is not typing into a computer for hours after every shift. On traction: The category leader in ambient clinical documentation, deployed across large American health systems. On money: A three hundred million dollar Series E led by Andreessen Horowitz and Khosla Ventures in April 2026, valuing it at five point three billion dollars, with a reported extension of a further three hundred and sixteen million. Why it matters: Ambient documentation is the first AI product hospitals bought at scale, and it won because it gave time back rather than replacing anyone. And the thing to steal: Sell the hour back to the person who hates their paperwork. That buyer signs quickly and stays.

meta.one_liner: Listens to the doctor's appointment and writes the medical note.

segments.heading: Mirendil
segments.subhead: Breakout / benchmark company · Breakout · AI research lab
segments.speak: Number 2 of 8. Mirendil. Autonomous systems that turn compute into scientific discoveries. Not in an accelerator batch. This one is on the list as a benchmark, because it is the company everyone else in its category is measured against. Mirendil is a research lab building self-accelerating systems for science - AI that runs the research loop itself across fields like biology and materials science, rather than assisting a human researcher. On traction: Founded in 2025 by Behnam Neyshabur, Harsh Mehta, Shayan Salehian and Tara Rezaei. On money: A two hundred million dollar seed round at a one billion dollar valuation, backed by Andreessen Horowitz, Nvidia, Kleiner Perkins and Neo. Why it matters: A two hundred million dollar seed at a billion-dollar valuation, on a research thesis with no product. That is the extreme end of this market. And the thing to steal: Reputation is now collateral. A team from the top of the research world can raise a Series B before writing a product.

meta.one_liner: Autonomous systems that turn compute into scientific discoveries.

segments.heading: SUN
segments.subhead: a16z Speedrun · SR006 · Consumer AI, audio
segments.speak: Number 3 of 8. SUN. Personalised podcasts and audiobooks you can interrupt and ask questions. Andreessen Horowitz Speedrun, SR006. SUN generates audio tailored to you - a podcast or audiobook built for your interests - and lets you talk back to it in real time, asking questions mid-listen and getting answers inside the same stream. On traction: A three-person team out of Harvard computer science, a Stanford AI PhD, and the founding engineer of Amazon Podcasts. Selected into the Andreessen Horowitz Speedrun sixth cohort. On money: Andreessen Horowitz Speedrun invests up to one million dollars, plus up to five million dollars in credits. Why it matters: This is precisely the format you are listening to right now, built as a company. Personalised, interruptible audio is a real emerging category. And the thing to steal: Worth watching closely if you ever want to build in this space - they are the closest competitor to your own daily brief.

meta.one_liner: Personalised podcasts and audiobooks you can interrupt and ask questions.

segments.heading: Sazabi
segments.speak: Number 4 of 8. Sazabi. Reads your production logs, works out why it broke, and ships the fix. Y Combinator, Winter 2026. When something breaks in production, Sazabi analyses the logs to find the cause, then generates the code fix and opens it for you in one click. It closes the loop between the alert and the patch. On traction: Called out as a Winter 2026 standout by multiple investors. On money: Y Combinator Winter 2026. Why it matters: Debugging production is where engineers actually lose their nights. This is the on-call engineer as a product. And the thing to steal: The winning agent products do not stop at the diagnosis. They deliver the fix.

meta.one_liner: Reads your production logs, works out why it broke, and ships the fix.

segments.heading: Superset
segments.speak: Number 5 of 8. Superset. Mission control for running a hundred coding agents at once. Y Combinator, Spring 2026. Superset centrally manages large fleets of coding agents, so a developer can run well over a hundred agent tasks in parallel and still know what each one is doing. On traction: Named among the standout companies of Spring 2026 by investors. On money: Y Combinator Spring 2026. Why it matters: One agent is a toy. A hundred agents is an operations problem, and operations problems are where durable software gets built. And the thing to steal: Whenever a unit becomes cheap and plentiful, the orchestration layer above it becomes valuable.

meta.one_liner: Mission control for running a hundred coding agents at once.

segments.heading: Ezra
segments.speak: Number 6 of 8. Ezra. The biggest tracked round to come out of the Speedrun portfolio this year. Andreessen Horowitz Speedrun, Speedrun alum. Ezra is the Speedrun alumnus that raised the largest tracked round in the portfolio recently, showing what the follow-on path out of the programme looks like when it works. On traction: A thirty-two million dollar seed round in March 2026 - the largest tracked Speedrun deal. On money: Thirty-two million dollar seed, March 2026. Why it matters: Speedrun's whole thesis is being the first cheque before a much larger seed. Ezra is the proof point. And the thing to steal: Accelerators are increasingly graded on the size of the round that follows, not the demo day.

meta.one_liner: The biggest tracked round to come out of the Speedrun portfolio this year.

segments.heading: Kira
segments.speak: Number 7 of 8. Kira. Water technology, in a cohort otherwise full of software. Andreessen Horowitz Speedrun, SR007. Kira is the water technology company in the current Speedrun batch - one of the few in a cohort where the overwhelming majority carry an AI tag and more than half sell to businesses. On traction: Speedrun SR007, currently running. On money: Andreessen Horowitz Speedrun SR007. Why it matters: Data centres consume enormous quantities of water. Water and power are becoming the same conversation. And the thing to steal: Being the only one of your kind in a cohort is a position, not a problem. You are the memorable pitch in the room.

meta.one_liner: Water technology, in a cohort otherwise full of software.

segments.heading: Librar Labs
segments.speak: Number 8 of 8. Librar Labs. AI library management for schools. Y Combinator, Winter 2026. Librar Labs handles cataloguing and inventory for school libraries, replacing decades-old systems that librarians hate and administrators never budget to replace. On traction: Named among the most interesting Winter 2026 companies. On money: Y Combinator Winter 2026. Why it matters: A reminder that small, ignored institutional markets still get funded when the software is obviously ten times better. And the thing to steal: You do not need a large market to start. You need a market where the current software is genuinely terrible.

segments.heading: The pattern
segments.speak: That's the companies. Now the pattern. Three things showed up more than once today: agents, devtools. When a theme repeats across companies that never met each other, that is usually the market telling you where the money is going. Sectors you just heard: AI, AI research lab, Climate, Consumer AI, Developer tools, Education software, Healthcare AI.

segments.heading: Your turn
segments.speak: That's the brief. Before you get out of the car, three questions. One. Take what Abridge is doing and ask who else has that exact problem but no budget for a specialist. That is usually the cheaper, faster version of the same company. Two. Of everything you just heard, which one could you build a rough version of this weekend? Not the whole thing. The single most annoying part of it. Three. Which of these companies would be trivial to beat in your own country or your own industry, because they will never bother to come here? Same time tomorrow. New companies.
